01.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the Sages of his day
01.event: The Sages sought to permit the Gibeonites to marry into the Jewish people.
01.turn: Rabbi objected that even if they could waive the people's share in the Gibeonites, no one could waive the altar's share.
01.summary: In the days of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, the Sages wanted to permit the Gibeonites to marry into the community. Rabbi stopped them: the court might give up the people's claim on the Gibeonites as servants, but who could give up the claim of the Temple altar?
01.missing: The text does not state explicitly that the proposal was dropped.

02.actor: Rav Mordekhai, reporting to Rav Ashi
02.event: A bill of divorce lay closer to the woman than to the husband and was lost, and the husband later died.
02.outcome: They required the woman to perform halitza, not relying on the divorce.
02.summary: Rav Mordekhai told Rav Ashi of an actual case: a bill of divorce was thrown nearer to the wife than to the husband and was then lost. When the husband died, the authorities did not treat her as divorced and required her to perform halitza.
02.missing: The details of the case are supplied only by the translator's gloss; the report itself is a bare one-line reference.

04.actor: Rav Nahman and a woman from Mehoza married to a man from Neharde'a
04.event: The couple came before Rav Nahman about her marriage contract, and he recognized her Mehoza accent and ruled by the custom of Babylonia, following Rav.
04.turn: They told him she was marrying into Neharde'a.
04.outcome: He reversed himself and ruled by Neharde'a's custom, following Shmuel.
04.summary: A woman from Mehoza married a man from Neharde'a, and they came before Rav Nahman about her marriage contract. Hearing her accent, he ruled according to the custom of Babylonia. When they pointed out that she was marrying into Neharde'a, he changed his ruling to follow Neharde'a's custom instead.

05.actor: A depositor, the late Hasa, and Rav Nahman
05.event: A man deposited a silver goblet with Hasa, who died without leaving instructions about it.
05.turn: Rav Nahman reasoned that Hasa was not wealthy enough to own such a goblet and that the claimant gave identifying marks.
05.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled in favor of the depositor, provided he was not a frequent visitor to the house.
05.summary: A man had left a silver goblet in Hasa's house, and Hasa died without saying anything about it. The case came to Rav Nahman, who said Hasa was known not to be rich and the claimant could describe the goblet, so the goblet went to the claimant, unless he was someone who regularly came and went there and could simply have seen it.

06.actor: A man preparing a feast, and Rava
06.event: A man prepared a betrothal feast on the ninetieth day after the woman's first husband died.
06.summary: A man prepared a feast for his betrothal on the ninetieth day after his bride's first husband had died. Rava forbade it, and the man's feast went to waste. The Gemara adds that it was really a wedding feast, not a betrothal feast.

07.event: Rav Hamnuna posed a challenge from a baraita, and Rava had no answer and fell silent.
07.turn: After Rav Hamnuna left, Rava thought of an answer, doubted it, and then found a baraita confirming it.
07.outcome: Rava concluded the challenge could be dismissed because the baraita follows Rabbi Elazar.
07.summary: Rav Hamnuna challenged Rava with a baraita, and Rava stood silent. Once Rav Hamnuna had gone, Rava asked himself why he had not answered that the baraita follows Rabbi Elazar. He doubted his own answer, then recalled a teaching showing Rabbi Elazar held so even in this case, which settled it for him.
07.missing: Rav Hamnuna's departure and the answer are never delivered to him; the encounter ends in Rava's own reflection.

08.event: A case came before Rabbi about an alleyway closed on one side by the sea and on the other by a garbage dump.
08.outcome: He said neither that carrying there was prohibited nor that it was permitted.
08.summary: An alleyway ran from the sea at one end to a garbage dump at the other, and the question of whether one could carry in it on Shabbat was brought to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. He gave no ruling at all, neither permitting nor forbidding it.

09.event: Aher saw the tongue of the executed Hutzpit the disseminator being dragged along by a pig.
09.turn: He cried out that a mouth that produced pearls should not lick the dust.
09.summary: According to one tradition, Elisha ben Avuya saw the tongue of the martyred teacher Hutzpit being dragged through the dirt by a pig. Appalled, he asked how a mouth that had spoken pearls could end up licking dust, and from then on he abandoned the faith and sinned.

11.actor: Unnamed people who weighed a turnip
11.event: A fox nested inside a turnip, and people weighed it.
11.turn: It turned out to weigh sixty litra even with the hollow.
11.summary: As proof that produce can grow enormous, the Sages recalled a turnip so large that a fox made its den inside it. When people weighed it, it came to sixty litra by the measure of Tzippori.
11.missing: It is cited only as a brief proof; there is no larger narrative or ending.

14.actor: Rav Nahman, Rav Adda bar Ahava and Rav Hana
14.event: Rav Nahman found Rav Adda bar Ahava and his son-in-law Rav Hana in the Pumbedita marketplace debating a mishna about a minor and a deaf-mute widow.
14.turn: Rav Nahman told them their distinction did not hold.
14.summary: Rav Nahman came upon Rav Adda bar Ahava and his son-in-law Rav Hana in the Pumbedita marketplace, trading arguments about when levirate marriage with one widow frees her co-wife. They proposed that if the dead brother was deaf-mute the question resolves itself; Rav Nahman told them it remains uncertain even then.
14.missing: The encounter is a frame for a legal argument; their reaction to Rav Nahman is not given.

15.actor: Ravina and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
15.event: Ravina found Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak leaning on a door bar, pondering a legal question.
15.summary: Ravina came upon Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak leaning on the bar of a door, lost in thought over whether a husband who says only "void" about a bill of divorce has cancelled it. No answer was found.
15.missing: There is a scene but no turn; it frames an unresolved legal question.

16.actor: Rav Yosef and two claimants holding deeds
16.event: Two deeds to the same property came before Rav Yosef, one dated the fifth of Nisan and one dated only Nisan, and he awarded the property to the fifth-of-Nisan holder.
16.turn: The losing claimant protested and then asked for a writ to repossess property sold from Iyyar onward.
16.outcome: Rav Yosef refused, since buyers could claim his deed dated from the first of Nisan.
16.summary: Two men brought deeds for the same property to Rav Yosef: one dated the fifth of Nisan, the other simply Nisan. Rav Yosef gave the property to the man with the exact date. When the other protested, he was told his deed could be from late in the month; when he then asked for a writ to collect from buyers after Iyyar, Rav Yosef said those buyers could argue his deed was from the first of Nisan, so he should claim the field itself.

18.actor: Rabba bar Avuh and Rav Nahman
18.event: Rabba bar Avuh told the Sages to examine Rav Nahman in the bathhouse, promising his daughter if his body gave off steam.
18.summary: Rabba bar Avuh, considering Rav Nahman as a husband for his daughter, told the Sages to watch him while bathing: if his flesh gave off steam, a sign of virility, he would give him his daughter.
18.missing: The result of the examination and whether the marriage happened.

19.actor: A man who fell into the Great Cistern; Rabbi Meir
19.event: A man fell into the Great Cistern and came out after three days.
19.summary: Rabbi Meir cited a case of a man who fell into the Great Cistern and came out alive three days later. The Sages objected that miracles are not used to decide law.
19.missing: The incident is only referenced by its opening words from the mishna; its full account is not in the segments shown.

20.actor: A man who betrothed a woman too early, and Rafram
20.event: A man betrothed a woman within three months of her divorce or widowhood and then fled.
20.outcome: Rafram ruled that his flight was punishment enough and he was not excommunicated.
20.summary: A man betrothed a woman during the three months she was required to wait, and then fled. When the case was brought to Rafram, he ruled that running away was enough of a penalty and no excommunication was needed.
20.missing: The incident is reported only as a bare case serving a legal dispute.
